inline.s: Since first I took refuge and circled the Dharma altar, I have begged at every hour for this mind to be at peace. Do not say we are parted by three thousand li — the moon stands at mid-heaven, and we meet face to face.

Now and then I take up rod and line and see my plain and simple heart; the bamboo-branch song done, how few are the listeners? The little boat goes home through a frosty night — where shall one seek the bright moon and the reed flowers?

In the cold sky the wild geese cry one by one, each voice alone; from today my traces fall among the Five Lakes. Boundless misty waves carry my sorrowful thoughts; a single sail on the horizon is the road home.

For the Dharma, how could I decline a distant road? How could I call this land of miasma the world’s end? Again and again I take one drop of Caoxi’s water to irrigate the five-petal flower that came from the West.
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Thirty-Eight
Gāthās, Part One
Elucidating Zou Sheng Ziyin: Ten Verses

This matter is utterly clear, with nothing hidden at all;
it stands revealed and magnificent through all heaven and across the earth.
If a true man does not pierce through with the vajra eye,
he faces a wall though he looks straight at it.

Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all flowers in the air;
while the film is not yet removed, one’s seeing only worsens.
Only when the eye is clear and pure as the open sky
does one come to know a different and better life.

In the realm of sound and form, how could it be by chance?
One takes up thorns and brambles and bitterly questions Heaven.
Who is it that casts all aside, turns over, and comes out?
Only then does he believe in the free and easy Chan that follows conditions.

The wondrous nature, perfect and bright, is true from the first;
from of old it is pure and bright, never stained by the finest dust.
Do not let deluded defilement lightly cloud and obstruct it:
just this is to be a man of great power who transcends the ordinary.

The mind of the Way was never apart from the ordinary;
why be so busy welcoming guests and greeting visitors?
Just look at the pivot within it all:
has it ever stirred by a single hair?

Deep and clear, the light of the mind is never deluded;
it is only that feeling and thought estrange it from itself.
Just see that where they rise there is no tidings at all,
and let the monkeys cry out by day and by night as they will.

The clouds of the nature-sky are clear, the moon’s disk alone;
why should body and world ask whether they exist or not?
Only let the traces of worldly ties be cut off,
and one need not labor to hang a name on rivers and lakes.

Worldly ties pursue us on and on — when will they ever cease?
One casts away one’s own home mountain and seeks outside.
The bright pearl lies buried in the hem of the robe,
while on the long road one vainly hugs one’s poverty and sorrow.

The lightning of the vast void spares nothing in its flash;
how could like and hate be allowed to march in file?
Split open the true face you were born with:
how could you let it pass your whole life buried?
To Yuan Sheng

Long ago I sent a letter south to Neng;
asking the Dharma, I paid court from afar to the supreme vehicle.
I know that samādhi may be entered through words —
I wonder, do you still recall the monk of former days?
To the Chan Monk Shuitian

How hard it is for a true teacher and a student to meet!
Within it the hidden message is hard to put into words.
On the summit of Wondrous Peak, along the track where you walked,
Sudhana was not taken in by empty talk.
To Tan Fuzhi

You once received the prediction at Vulture Peak;
today you come again and give one knock at the gate.
I ask you about the matter of the twirled flower that day —
the ascetic is no easy man to please.
To Zhong Sheng Hengying

Ten years have passed since you visited Caoxi;
to meet a true teacher is all former affinity.
Why should Ruan weep at the end of the road?
The supreme Chan that came from the West is yours already.
To the Scholar Fang Juezhi

The light of the mind shines out alone beyond the body;
you can fathom the Patriarch’s intent before a word is spoken.
I think you have heard Mount Kuang’s lotus water-clock till it ripened,
and so you come to renew the old affinity.
To the Chan Monk Changda
To the Chan Monk Zongxuan

Illusorily formed, the five aggregates are empty from the first;
to insist on seeking them is to catch the wind.
Just try, once body and mind have wholly dissolved,
to recognize and take hold of the master within.
To the Hermitage Master Yongzhi of Nanyue

Deep among ten thousand mountains, one thatched hut;
morning and evening the clouds and rosy light serve as my little assembly.
Above all, the voice of the stream cannot be shut away:
with its broad and long tongue it murmurs day and night.
Dwelling in the Mountains at Nanyue

Seventy years have passed like a dream;
my traces on rivers and lakes are all squandered and astray.
Now I am glad to have gained this idle field of ground —
ask nothing of how things were before.

My heels have trodden every water-and-cloud land,
yet I have never left the ancient place of the Way at Qingliang.
My strength fails and my mind is already weary:
to sleep well and eat my fill is my whole way of living.

The place of great rest and cessation is nothing ordinary;
when deluded thought subsides, the world is already forgotten.
People all seek the true Land of Ultimate Bliss elsewhere —
who knows that this very moment is the West?

One only sees the unborn, still and extinguished mind;
deluded thoughts find no way to invade it.
The senses and their objects are all shadows of flowers in the air —
why seek the Buddhas and Patriarchs outside?

Watch where the mind arises: it is utterly unborn.
In the flash of lightning the eye grows doubly bright.
I ask what the coming from the West was meant to accomplish —
the people of today understand only how to hurry on their way.
To the Monk Mijie of Luling

How stands the price of rice in Luling these days?
When you are asked, do not just repeat what others say.
If you can lightly chew and break a single grain,
you will know the Buddhadharma is no great matter.
To the Chan Monk Duyan

The Chan of Master Ma, one stream of the Western River —
I hear its transmission has long been lost.
Do not say a brick can be ground into a mirror;
of itself it will not fall to the byways of the road.
To the Chan Monk Dingshui

For long I have relied on the flower throne to seek the true meaning;
bell and drum are clear, and phrase by phrase is profound.
If you ask the precise purport of the coming from the West —
from of old the Buddhas and Patriarchs have never transmitted it.
To the Chan Monk Liangkong, Who Receives Guests at Wuchang

I hear a Brahma monastery has opened by the river’s edge,
just when the coming and going winds and sails are crossing.
I ask the fisherman who casts his line at Huating:
how many know the three inches between hook and bait?
Inscribed on Fang Juezhi’s Hut of Freedom from Defilement

In a hermitage the size of a mustard seed, not a speck of dust;
from the first there has been nothing one could draw near to.
In quiet contemplation, the cool ground of stillness and cessation —
suddenly one sees the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body.
Inscribed on the Kṣānti Hermitage

Self and things are empty as space and cannot be sought;
they are a single floating bubble on the boundless sea.
Just look: where they rise there is no trace at all —
let suffering and joy come to rest right where they are.
To the Chan Monk Tianyuan

The matter beneath your own body and mind is perfectly clear;
no need to seek a teacher and wear yourself out in far travel.
Only take it up intimately right before your eyes —
who is it that sees forms and hears sounds?
To the Chan Monk Liuyi
Sent to Dharma Master Ruomei

One who dwells in a hut below Lotus Peak,
day by day befriending the Five Elders in the clouds.
The waterfall scatters jade dust through the air,
as if host and guest were sitting in talk together.
To the Chan Monk Changyuan of Yunju

Leaving the world is at root for the sake of fathoming this mind,
not for the sake of hanging a name in the monastery groves.
When the huatou is pressed to the place of no-mind,
one does not seek it outside in another’s house.
Sent to the Master of the Haihui Hermitage
Reply to Dharma Master Yu, Who Sent a New Commentary on the Lotus Sutra

The one assembly at Vulture Peak required much deliberation,
and for more than forty years it lay covered and hidden.
Today the whole body is utterly exposed —
clearly it lies in a single hair’s tip.

The gate is shut fast, and no wind passes through;
how many pace and sigh, lamenting that the road is ended?
It is not that a light snap of the fingers is much trouble —
how else would one know that what lies within is vast as space?

When the poor son came home and saw his father,
he entrusted his heart to him and believed without doubt.
Yet even if the whole treasury were handed over to him,
unless he overturn it, he will never know it at all.

The boundless ocean of Buddha-lands is all lotus flowers;
one may sigh that in former days they were counted as grains of sand.
If you point it out for yourself at the tip of a hair,
from today you will always drive the white ox cart.
To the Chan Monk Supu (with a preface)

This monk once came to consult me at Caoxi, and afterwards returned to Wumen. Not long ago the two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu, because I and his own teacher Xuelang were brothers in the Dharma gate, had this monk carry a letter and travel far to Nanyue to invite me to spend my last years there. Moved by the lofty friendship of these two masters, and mindful of this monk’s long toil, I composed two gāthās to record what was in my heart.

I once bowed at Caoxi and walked the land of miasma,
circumambulated three times in reverence, and circled the Chan bed.
The single phrase of the unborn was perfectly clear —
do not say that anything was concealed then.

From afar I bring a letter from an old friend,
and come especially to these empty hills to ask where I might dwell.
This whole body and mind I entrust to you entirely;
there is no need to ask what my remaining years will be.
Reply to the Two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu

The righteous spirit of the Dharma gate is truly beyond the ordinary;
of itself the green mountain has the fragrance of bone and flesh.
I mean to go up to the summit of Tongxuan Peak,
and there face you wordlessly on one rope bed.

The mountains and waters of Wumen are the most secluded and clear;
the twin peaks of Erlang have long been famed.
If only we might share the mist and rosy clouds and grow old together,
sleeping well and eating our fill would see out the rest of our lives.
To the Chan Monk Fucha

From afar I ask after Lanzan among a thousand peaks;
the cold tears at the corner of his mouth have never dried.
The yellow yam in the fire has just been roasted through —
to set it before you is no easy meal.
To the Chan Monk Dazhi

With bamboo staff and straw sandals I crossed ten thousand mountains,
coming from Nanyue to knock at the pine gate.
On Shitou’s road, slippery, it is hard to move a step;
do not say that travelling to seek instruction is a light matter.
Inscribed on the Scroll of Meeting at Biefeng
Inquiring After the Illness of Zhuan Yu, Master Heng

The four great elements I have long seen as bubbles and shadows;
where could the demon of illness hide its traces?
The ancients had their own way of resting at ease:
it lies in a single thought of the unborn.
To the Chan Monk Ruozhuo

You have walked to the ends of the earth seeking this mind,
yet from the first you have always sought it outside.
Even before you take a step beyond the gate,
trust that the grass grows deeper the farther the road runs.
Sent to Xu Beng’e

From time to time I ask after Vimalakīrti in his illness;
the door opens on non-duality and reveals the natural truth.
Having eaten the fragrant rice to the full, words forgotten,
one only then believes that with feeling put aside, the Way at last draws near.
To the Chan Monk Xinwen

The original self-nature is vast as space;
seeing forms and hearing sounds is a tree passing through wind.
Only let the floating clouds be wholly scattered,
and when has a single thing ever lodged within it?
To the Chan Monk Sanmei Zhen, on His Pilgrimage to Emei

You have travelled through all quarters; it is well to let the mind rest.
It was no vain thing to hang your name in the monastery groves.
When you return, your face will be covered with Emei snow —
white clouds and green hills, where shall they be sought?
To the Master of Jing Mountain

Lightning flash and flint spark — how could these be real?
A glance of meeting is not yet something to draw near to.
If the original tidings are truly cut off,
the whole great chiliocosm appears in your body wherever you stand.
The Chan Monk Yeyin Went from Huangmei to Nanyue and Then to Consult at Shuangjing; I Showed Him This Gāthā

You travelled far to Nanyue seeking your traces,
and I am glad that one thread of Huangmei has come through.
Elsewhere, at the place of meeting on the Five Peaks,
snows of ten thousand mountains surround a white-haired old man.
To the Chan Monk Wuxia

With staff in hand you came from afar to the deep places of Shuangjing;
to meet at a separate peak is to meet a kindred spirit.
If old friends ask about the rest of my life:
ten thousand folded ranges of cloud, and one single heart.
To the Lay Buddhist Nianxi

You have travelled south over misty waters through a hundred cities;
to meet a true teacher — what did it come to?
Seek still deeper in the Five Peaks:
you should know the Buddhadharma is no great matter.
To the Chan Monk Qinru, on His Pilgrimage to Emei

From Shuangjing far away you bow at Emei;
you cross waters and climb mountains — for whose sake?
If you see Samantabhadra’s true face,
do not fail that pair of brows.
To the Hall Master of Jing Mountain

At Shuangjing the single transmission of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ mind;
grey cliffs and green bamboo, an ancient monastery grove.
You should know that where the true command is ever new,
bell and drum proclaim the wondrous sound of the Dharma.
In Memoriam: Master Huanyu

On the cold cliff, frozen and starving — who knew of it?
After seeming death you were revived again, and I owe it to you, Master.
Today, gazing at the pagoda’s shadow on the Five Peaks,
it is as if we still sat talking face to face.
To Dharma Master Ren’an

Body and mind are one piece, like a jar of ice;
try to see whether anything is there within it.
When deluded thoughts do not come and the tidings are cut off,
why seek your practice anywhere beyond this?
Passing the Bodhi Hermitage, I Happily Met the Chan Friend Zhihe

You were originally a man beneath the bodhi tree;
when you arrived, in a flash I seemed to see my former body.
The voice of the stream always preaches the unborn Dharma —
pity that the people of today do not hear it truly.
To the Chan Monk Xunnan, Who Tends the Sick

What is the most excellent cause for leaving the world?
To see through, right before your eyes, this body in illness.
Know the place where his pain and itching are bound up with yours —
of all ten thousand practices, none is truer than this one thought.
To the Chan Monk Demen, Who Collates Sutras

The eye of the sea has never held a speck of dust;
the great treasury of light is a place where one may rest.
Only look carefully from the very beginning:
the moment a fine mote clings, the truth is lost.
To the Chan Monk Feixuan Xiao

You once studied the teachings at Cien and ordered their framework;
then you threw away the fishing rod and travelled through all quarters.
If today you recognize the face you were born with,
there is no need to ask the Dharma King with your mind.
Passing the Sweet Dew Reception Temple

Climbing mountains and wading waters, all is a road gone astray;
who knows whether there is a village ahead or not?
Then straight on I suddenly met the sprinkling of sweet dew —
but one drop touched me and my scorched dryness broke.
To the Chan Monk Chengzhuo, Who Holds the Vidyā and Practices in Secret

Fierce flames blaze, and deluded thoughts pour forth;
the clarified butter must be poured upon the crown of the head.
When a single drop has reached every pore,
only then is it the secret cultivation of holding the vidyā.
At the Danbo Studio, Shown to the Lay Buddhist Yunshan
